Subscribe another address How a plan to turn the Spokane Spokesman-Review into “The People’s Paper” ended in a newsroom revolt Newsroom staffers say that concerns about Rob Curley’s leadership festered until his August suspension — weeks before the paper was set to transfer to his nonprofit. Rob Curley, executive editor of the Spokesman-Review in Spokane, Washington, speaking at the 2023 News Media Mega-Conference. (scottcornelius.com ) By Wilson Criscione, InvestigateWest and Daisy Zavala Magaña, RANGE Oct. 5, 2026, 2:44 p.m. This report was produced in a collaboration between InvestigateWest and RANGE . When the Spokesman-Review announced plans to transfer Spokane’s 143-year-old, family-owned newspaper to a nonprofit founded by executive editor Rob Curley, it took over the front page. “The People’s Paper,” read the April 16, 2025, headline, saying ownership would transfer “to you, the community.” Key to the plan was Curley, the folksy self-proclaimed “journalism nerd” who burst into Spokane a decade ago, declaring a love for Gonzaga University basketball rivaled only by his love for Disney. The transition to Comma Community Journalism Lab was cast in media industry publications not only as a way to save Spokane’s daily newspaper, but as part of a growing movement to resurrect dying papers by making them less dependent on ads and corporate ownership and more on philanthropy and community partnerships. As proof of concept, the paper had already added several so-called “community-funded” journalists to its staff. But in the Spokesman-Review newsroom this summer, that hopeful vision ran into persistent concerns about Curley’s leadership. More than a dozen current and former employees, along with contemporaneous records reviewed by InvestigateWest and RANGE, reveal how the newsroom had raised concerns about Curley’s management for years, culminating in his suspension from the paper on Aug. 7 and a vote of no confidence from the union, the Spokane Editorial Society. He is currently on leave as the paper conducts an internal investigation. Employees said stories that might have angered powerful community figures or potential donors were killed or curtailed, and that they felt he retaliated against workers he viewed as disloyal. Staffers questioned his financial oversight of Comma, which hired his own son at a salary topping most reporters’ and recruited out-of-town executives to serve as top editors before Comma had met its fundraising goal. Current and former Spokesman-Review employees also described workplace complaints involving Curley and one of those editors, including allegations of inappropriate lewd and sexual comments around employees, including teenage interns. Curley declined to comment for this article. In a brief phone interview, Curley’s attorney, Patrick Kirby, who specializes in employment and wrongful termination cases, said, “It’s all inaccurate,” in reference to a list of claims InvestigateWest and RANGE provided to Curley prior to publication. Kirby hung up the call when a reporter pressed him on which claims specifically he believed were inaccurate. The top of Page 1 of The Spokesman-Review, April 16, 2025. Tensions in the newsroom came to a head in the first week of August, as the paper rallied to cover the most destructive wildfires in Spokane’s history and the imminent ownership transfer approached at the end of the month. Some staffers were alarmed at the prospect of working for an organization Curley founded, with even fewer checks on his authority. “The terror had been building through advertising, circulation, and this newsroom each day, getting closer to the day of knowing we would have to work for Rob without the filter of human resources and the publisher,” said one employee, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution. Reporters had grown increasingly frustrated with Comma editors meddling with stories, and Curley tried to fire a reporter who pushed back, employees say. But instead, when other Spokesman-Review editors backed the reporter, publisher William “Stacey” Cowles suspended Curley, citing “ several personnel complaints ” against him. It wasn’t until after Curley’s suspension that reporters were told news that called the Comma plan into question. In a meeting days after Curley had been kicked out of the building, Spokesman-Review management shared that despite public claims by Curley that several reporters were paid for by community donors — a source of optimism for the Comma plan — none of the paper’s reporting positions were currently community-funded. There were “audible gasps,” according to several reporters in the room. The paper had been promoting its community-funded reporters online, removing paywalls for stories written by those journalists. One reporter remembered how at fundraising events, Curley would point to a journalist’s face on a big screen and tell donors that their money paid for journalists’ salaries. Even the reporters took pride in sharing the claim with readers. “I’ve been lying on his behalf without even knowing it,” one reporter said. Cowles, the publisher, said he had no comment on the claims about Curley until the conclusion of the internal investigation. He said the paper is targeting Oct. 30 to close the transaction with Comma. Bill Simer, Comma Community Journalism Lab board chair, did not comment for this article. Saving local journalism Before joining the Spokesman-Review in 2016, Curley had been praised in some journalism circles as a leader in transitioning struggling newspapers away from print and into the digital world. In naming Curley as the Spokesman-Review’s new top editor, Cowles said Curley had “a proven record of delivering news that matters” and that his “innovative work” at previous newspapers helped them win top journalism awards “including a Pulitzer Prize,” the announcement said. But reporters at his previous gigs viewed him differently : as a mercurial leader who hyped expensive, ineffective initiatives, sacrificing journalism ethics to keep up cozy relationships with powerful community institutions and politicians. The Orange County Register in Southern California was criticized for favorable coverage of Disney under Curley, who served as the paper’s top editor between 2014 and 2016 and proudly said he wore a Mickey Mouse garment every day. He also faced backlash when he revised an article two months after it had been published at the request of a politician, despite police reports and other records that didn’t support the change . Curley changed the story over the objections of the reporter and did not note the changes for the public with a correction or editor’s note — a decision journalism ethicists called an “unethical overreach.” Journalists from the Las Vegas Sun in Nevada had their own problems with him. After he left the Sun in 2012, they noticed that Curley kept getting credit for the paper’s Pulitzer Prize in 2009 — credit that Cowles repeated in the 2016 hiring announcement. Sun employees clarified to the Inlander, a Spokane alt-weekly, that Curley, in fact, had nothing to do with the series that won the Pulitzer. Curley said he’d never told anyone he won a Pulitzer, blaming a series of misunderstandings for it showing up time and time again in his biography. Curley stuck around Spokane, undaunted by the controversies from his past. And with layoffs and buyouts shrinking the newsroom in a struggling industry, Curley two years ago began testing the Comma pitch among staff by signaling that it would save their jobs. Reporters said he told them privately that they’d receive big raises once the transfer happened. If Comma didn’t move forward, he said the Cowles family would likely lay off staff or maybe sell the locally owned paper to one of the hedge fund–owned companies known for downsizing newsrooms, one current employee recalled. Reporters felt Curley had compromised editorial independence at the Spokesman as well. Staffers took issue with Curley altering an article in 2025 about a bond proposal from Spokane Public Schools. In the article, reporters wrote a passage explaining how the proposal could raise property taxes. The story had been cleared by the typical story editors, but late the night before the story was published, Curley had a copy editor change that passage “to be more in line with what the school district wanted us to be saying,” said Emry Dinman, one of the article’s two reporters. “My editors were all as outraged as I was.” Staffers knew Comma was trying to partner with the school district as part of the ownership transition, though Dinman said he didn’t want to speculate on the intentions behind the late-night edit. Current and former staffers also said Curley didn’t like articles that were critical of Gonzaga, a private university downtown most known for its basketball team that Curley frequently celebrated in his columns. Rebecca Hansen-White, a former reporter at the Spokesman-Review from 2018 to 2020, said that during the COVID-19 pandemic she wrote a story about Gonzaga’s plans for an isolation facility, which included some light criticism from a local politician for the private university using government money to do so. But the story was never published. When Hansen-White asked what happened, she recalls an editor told her something to the effect of “that may have been one Rob didn’t want to run,” though she was never able to confirm if Curley spiked it himself. “That was very frustrating. I worked hard on this and I’m going out to the community and I’m getting in these tough conversations with sources,” she said. “And then I come back to the newsroom and find that my work has been changed or removed without an explanation.” Comma eventually set up shop on the Gonzaga campus in 2024 . The two editors who Curley hired for Comma in fall 2025 did little to ease reporter concerns about outside interference. Donna Wares and Ron Sylvester had both worked with Curley at the Orange County Register, and when Curley brought them into the Spokesman-Review newsroom, an email sent to the staff described their roles until the transfer as “consultants” — Sylvester for “newsroom metrics and trust initiatives,” and Wares for “enterprise story assignment, editing and Northwest Passages author recruitment.” Northwest Passages is the nonprofit’s book club and event series. That distinction was crucial for Spokesman-Review staffers, who considered it a breach of journalistic integrity to have non-staffers weigh in on editorial decisions, even if it came from people who would one day be their editors. “We were told through the union that Comma editors would not be able to touch our stories until the transition happened,” said Emily White, a former reporter who left the Spokesman at the end of August. But that’s not what happened. “They were tampering with our stories with no permission,” White said. The union filed a grievance with the company, said Thomas Clouse, union president and longtime reporter. “Our understanding was that the publisher dealt with it,” he said. A newsroom altercation As Comma took longer than initially expected to reach its $2 million fundraising goal, the transition kept being delayed. The presence of Comma staff in the newsroom, meanwhile, grew louder. Comma had also hired one of Curley’s sons. Johnathan Curley made a salary of $62,400, according to a 2025 court document, topping the pay of almost every Spokesman-Review reporter. His title at Comma is “technical director,” and he handles video and audio equipment for Comma events. Previously, the 24-year-old worked as a part-time audio-visual technician for Cirque du Soleil in Las Vegas. Johnathan Curley did not respond to requests for comment. Staffers questioned how much Sylvester and Wares were getting paid to be Comma editors before the transition, and they were concerned that Wares spent half her time in California, flying back and forth on Comma’s dime. Sylvester lingered in the newsroom, with staff increasingly unclear of his role. Employees described Sylvester as a disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office. He was tasked with managing the summer internship program, they said, but his involvement was so marginal that other staff had to pick up his slack. “If you ask what his job entailed, I wouldn’t be able to give you an answer,” one staffer said. Sylvester did not respond to requests for comment. In early August, with the planned transition to Comma just weeks away, the newsroom scrambled to cover wildfires that had caught national attention. The staff worked day and night, eventually breaking the news that one of the blazes was set by an arsonist. Courts reporter Alexandra Duggan, as it turned out, had been one of the first people to see the alleged arsonist near the flames. The Review Building, which houses the Spokesman-Review office, in downtown Spokane, Washington on September 30, 2026. (Wilson Criscione/InvestigateWest) On Aug. 4, Sylvester told reporters they should change how they attribute documents in stories. Instead of citing “court documents,” he said they should cite “sworn affidavits.” Despite having no clear editorial role in the Spokesman-Review newsroom, Sylvester went into Duggan’s story that night and made a change reflecting his preference — except in that instance, the record was not in fact an affidavit. It introduced an error into the paper. Clouse, the union president, said he called a meeting with management to try to understand why Comma editors were meddling with stories again. “That never got resolved,” he said. Two days later, Duggan, who’d worked 13 straight days, was finishing up another story about the accused arsonist. Sylvester approached her and said, in a low voice, “you’re doing it again,” several employees who witnessed or learned of the altercation told InvestigateWest and RANGE. He’d been referring to her story saying “court documents.” Duggan walked away. But Sylvester followed, and the two shouted back and forth at each other until other editors stepped in to cool things down. “I wanted to make sure that our stories were truthful and honest and that they were not being edited without us knowing and without any communication,” Duggan said. “And I just wanted to keep the integrity of the paper.” Curley sided with Sylvester, telling Spokesman-Review managing editor Lindsey Treffry that night to fire Duggan. Treffry refused. The next morning, during a series of meetings with Cowles, Treffry and other editors shared complaints they had about Curley. Cowles decided to put Curley on administrative leave, revoking his keycard access to the paper’s offices. A few hours later, however, Curley got in the newsroom again by asking an unsuspecting intern for their keycard. He walked around asking where he could find Treffry, who, according to several staffers there that day, was hiding from Curley in the photo room with other editors. Duggan joined them, and it was there that Duggan learned Treffry saved her job. As they hid, Duggan texted White, who was not in the newsroom at the time. White shared the texts with InvestigateWest and RANGE that described how an HR employee escorted Curley out of the building. “They chased Rob out of the newsroom,” Duggan texted. “I can’t see because I’m hiding.” “I’m hysterical,” Duggan wrote, crumpled into a ball and crying. Duggan said she’d “ride or die for this paper.” She said Curley’s attempt to fire her “felt like a slap in the face — it felt like betrayal.” In an interview for this story, she said she’ll be grateful for the rest of her life that Treffry had her back. “She did save my job. And she protected the rest of us from something similar,” Duggan said. “Jessica Rabbit” Former reporter Rachel Alexander, who worked at the Spokesman-Review from October 2014 to July 2018, recalled a pattern of “cronyism and ethics violations.” In a letter she sent to investigators after Curley’s suspension, Alexander described a departure of women on staff and in leadership roles during Curley’s first year; editors who left meetings with him looking “shaken, exhausted and at times afraid”; and how Curley didn’t keep promises to sponsor a former staff member’s work visa if he left the union. “Despite the meaningful journalism I was able to do and the presence of many talented colleagues who I greatly admire, I could not in good conscience continue working for a man who was willing to lie to a friend and jeopardize his ability to remain in the country,” Alexander wrote. “I made the decision to leave the Spokesman in 2018 primarily because of Mr. Curley’s behavior.” Before leaving, Alexander noticed that she was “nearly the only woman left on the desk,” according to her letter. She also told investigators that Curley seemed to primarily “take issue with or pick fights” with women in the newsroom. Instead of talking through concerns, he made “petty” decisions, like blocking reporters on Twitter, she wrote. In recent years, the paper has hosted high school interns as part of Curley’s effort to make Comma into a training ground for young journalists. But the behavior of Curley and Sylvester made some employees question whether they should be responsible for mentoring young journalists. One letter shared with internal investigators described how, during a 2024 barbecue for Spokesman-Review interns at Curley’s house, two teenage interns saw sexually explicit images of women on Curley’s iPad as he scrolled through his camera roll. Curley had been giving the high school girls a tour of his home and showing off his guitar collection. He was looking for song lyrics on his iPad when the inappropriate pictures flashed on his screen, according to employees who had heard of the incident from the interns. Several staff members also brought concerns to HR about inappropriate comments Sylvester made around interns who were in high school and college. In a conversation with another employee about the evolution of photography — and while sitting near an 18-year-old intern — Sylvester joked that if someone wanted to send a “dick pic” back in the day, they had to wait for it to develop, but today it can be done in an instant. On a different occasion, Sylvester told another employee to wait a few seconds before downloading porn, according to several employees. It was loud enough for other employees to hear the unprompted comment, including nearby interns. “It was very shocking to hear someone … who was supposed to be a mentor figure say that,” a staffer who witnessed the exchange said. “It’s just not appropriate for the workplace.” Current and former staff members also described a work environment where people perceived as being against Curley or who reported issues to HR were retaliated against. They felt Curley had favorites — including Sylvester and Wares — who would not face consequences for their actions. After an employee reported Sylvester to HR for his comment about dick pics, a letter to investigators said Curley appeared to retaliate against those he believed had made the report. Curley excluded one of the employees from important meetings and avoided another employee and gave them “distasteful looks.” Curley needed to make sure staff was “loyal” to him, employees said. They’re not in ours”: USA Today Co. execs defend Palantir deal Link fastcompany.com ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck October 8, 2026 USA Today Co. executives are revealing new details about a controversial deal with Palantir . In a joint interview with Fast Company’s Alex Pasternack , three executives from the country’s largest newspaper chain explained why they moved ahead with the Palantir deal despite major opposition from their own employees . RELATED ARTICLE “An inherent conflict of interest”: More than 800 USA Today Co. employees want the company to end its new Palantir partnership Hanaa' Tameez August 10, 2026 Mike Reed , the chairman and CEO of USA Today Co., previously said that the deal — first reported by Nieman Lab’s Hanaa’ Tameez — is part of a larger shift the company is making to become “an intelligence organization.” At a Palantir conference last month, Reed said that the company’s services were a way for USA Today Co. capitalize on “the shift to online and the data we have on consumers,” Pasternack reported. In this new interview, USA Today Media president Kristin Roberts detailed some of those services for the first time: In all of our entertainment stories and our sports stories, we do affiliate links to our partners. So if you’re reading a sports story, you want to buy the jersey for that team, our reporters and editors used to have to go to a file, find a relevant link, copy that link, put it in. All of that is now automated, and that’s a Palantir project. Lark-Marie Anton , then a communications executive at USA Today Co., chimed in, saying that Palantir’s current scope of work is focused on audience and advertising, but in the future that could extend to social media strategy and reporting tools. What stood out about Palantir was its ability to create what it calls an ‘ontology’ layer — essentially a unified model that allows different datasets and systems to work together and be acted upon in real time….The challenge isn’t collecting more data, but making better use of the data we already have. In August, more than 800 USA Today Co. employees from 31 unionized newsrooms called on the company to dissolve its partnership with Palantir. In a statement, staffers named ethical issues and uncertainty over how the software would be used . Throughout the Fast Company interview, Reed and Roberts heavily criticized the NewsGuild and internal efforts to oppose the deal. Roberts leveled the strongest criticisms of USA Today Co.’s unions across the country, going as far as to say the NewsGuild was lying to its members: Guild leadership is saying things that are factually untrue. They prey on fear. No matter that I will appear in front of any newsroom for a standup in which they ask me anything for an hour and a half at a time, and I explain to them all of the things. She continued: I’ll give you an example that’s incredibly real for us. Palantir doesn’t work inside of any USA Today Company system. They don’t have access to any of the notes our reporters take. They’re not in the Microsoft suite of tools. They don’t have information directly about our consumers or our staff….They don’t work in our systems. We feed them highly controlled data. We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours. Reed doubled down on these accusations, extending them to the work the NewsGuild has done organizing around AI in the company, including its push for clauses that would protect journalists from layoffs due to AI adoption. “I think we’re having more success in newsrooms that are not unionized, with this new world, than those that are unionized,” Reed said. Last month, USA Today Co. made significant layoffs across the company , including at its local newspapers, and reorganized its audience team. Reed, in a memo to staff , referenced AI-related traffic declines as a reason for the layoffs. “USA Today Co. executives’ animosity toward their workers and unions is nothing new,” said NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss in a statement to Fast Company. “[We] fully stand behind the statement workers released when this deal with Palantir was first announced.” You can read the full interview on Fast Company. Google’s News AI pilot expands to over 400 publications, including U.S. local news outlets Link blog.google ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide. At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes. RELATED ARTICLE Discover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippets Andrew Deck January 26, 2026 As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media ; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune . “People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab. Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “ pay-per-value ” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday .) With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.” An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines. Users can select the topics they’re most interested in hearing about, including “World,” “Gaming,” or “Sports” news. The feature includes citations that link to articles mentioned in the briefing. Subscribe another address From bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news” Link localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu ↗ Posted by Sophie Culpepper October 13, 2026 RELATED ARTICLE In Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than ever Sophie Culpepper October 22, 2025 If you thought last year was bleak , Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder. What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin , founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.” In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged. Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report. “When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states. RELATED ARTICLE Last year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s going Sophie Culpepper February 9, 2026 Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024. “Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois . “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.” The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left. A few other highlights from this year’s report: The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas. Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022. Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit . The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms. Read more in the full report here . Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap: Center of Excellence Feedback Summarize this article for me Note This article forms part of the Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap series of articles. For an overview of the series, see Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap . A data or analytics Center of Excellence (COE) is an internal team of technical and business experts. The team actively assists others within the organization who are working with data. The COE forms the nucleus of the broader community to advance adoption goals, which align with the data culture vision. A COE might also be known as competency center , capability center , or a center of expertise . Some organizations use the term squad . Many organizations perform the COE responsibilities within their data, analytics, or business intelligence (BI) team. Note Having a COE team formally recognized in your organizational chart is recommended, but not required. What's most important is that the COE roles and responsibilities are identified, prioritized, and assigned. It's common for a centralized data or analytics team to take on many of the COE responsibilities; some responsibilities might also reside within IT. For simplicity, in this series of articles, COE means a specific group of people , although you might implement it differently. It's also very common to implement the COE with a scope broader than Fabric or Power BI alone: for instance, a Power Platform COE, a data COE, or an analytics COE. Goals for a COE Goals for a COE include: Evangelizing a data-driven culture. Promoting the adoption of analytics. Nurturing, mentoring, guiding, and educating internal users to increase their skills and level of self-reliance. Coordinating efforts and disseminating knowledge across organizational boundaries. Creating consistency and transparency for the user community, which reduces friction and pain points related to finding relevant data and analytics content. Maximizing the benefits of self-service BI, while reducing the risks. Reducing technical debt by helping users make good decisions that increase consistency and result in fewer inefficiencies. Important One of the most powerful aspects of a COE is the cross-departmental insight into how analytics tools like Fabric are used by the organization. This insight can reveal which practices work well and which don't, that can facilitate a bottom-up approach to governance. A primary goal of the COE is to learn which practices work well, share that knowledge more broadly, and replicate best practices across the organization. Scope of COE responsibilities The scope of COE responsibilities can vary significantly between organizations. In a way, a COE can be thought of as a consultancy service because its members routinely provide expert advice to the internal community of users. To varying degrees, most COEs handle hands-on work too. Common COE responsibilities include: Mentoring and facilitating knowledge sharing within the internal Fabric community. Holding office hours to engage with the internal Fabric community. Conducting co-development projects and best practices reviews in order to actively help business units deliver solutions. Managing the centralized portal . Producing, curating, and promoting training materials . Creating documentation and other resources, such as template files , to encourage consistent use of standards and best practices. Applying, communicating, and assisting with governance guidelines. Handling and assisting with system oversight and Fabric administration. Responding to user support issues escalated from the help desk. Developing solutions and/or proofs of concept. Establishing and maintaining the BI platform and data architecture. Communicating regularly with the internal community of users. Staffing a COE People who are good candidates as COE members tend to be those who: Understand the analytics vision for the organization. Have a desire to continually improve analytics practices for the organization. Have a deep interest in, and expertise with, analytics tools such as Fabric. Are interested in seeing Fabric used effectively and adopted successfully throughout the organization. Take the initiative to continually learn, adapt, and grow. Readily share their knowledge with others. Are interested in repeatable processes, standardization, and governance with a focus on user enablement. Are hyper-focused on collaboration with others. Are comfortable working in an agile fashion. Have an inherent interest in being involved and helping others. Can effectively translate business needs into solutions. Communicate well with both technical and business colleagues. Tip If you have self-service content creators in your organization who constantly push the boundaries of what can be done, they might be a great candidate to become a recognized champion , or perhaps even a satellite member of the COE. When recruiting for the COE, it's important to have a mix of complementary analytical skills, technical skills, and business skills. Roles and responsibilities Very generalized roles within a COE are listed below. It's common for multiple people to overlap roles, which is useful from a backup and cross-training perspective. It's also common for the same person to serve multiple roles. For instance, most COE members also serve as a coach or mentor. Role Description COE leader Manages the day-to-day operations of the COE. Interacts with the executive sponsor and other organizational teams, such as the data governance board, as necessary. For an overview of additional roles and responsibilities, see the Governance article. Coach Coaches and educates others on data and BI skills via office hours (community engagement), best practices reviews , or co-development projects . Oversees and participates in the discussion channel of the internal community. Interacts with, and supports, the champions network . Trainer Develops, curates, and delivers internal training materials, documentation, and resources. Data analyst Domain-specific subject matter expert. Acts as a liaison between the COE and the business unit. Content creator for the business unit. Assists with content certification. Works on co-development projects and proofs of concept. Data modeler Creates and manages data assets (such as shared semantic model and dataflows (legacy)) to support other self-service content creators. Report creator Creates and publishes reports, dashboards, and metrics. Data engineer Plans for deployment and architecture, including integration with other services and data platforms. Publishes data assets which are utilized broadly across the organization (such as a lakehouse, data warehouse, data pipeline, dataflow, or semantic model). User support Assists with the resolution of data discrepancies and escalated help desk support issues. As mentioned previously, the scope of responsibilities for a COE can vary significantly between organizations. Therefore, the roles found for COE members can vary too. Structuring a COE The selected COE structure can vary among organizations. It's also possible for multiple structures to exist inside of a single large organization. That's particularly true when there are subsidiaries or when acquisitions have occurred. Note The following terms might differ to those defined for your organization, particularly the meaning of federated , which tends to have many different IT-related meanings. Centralized COE A centralized COE comprises a single shared services team. Pros : There's a single point of accountability for a single team that manages standards, best practices, and delivery end-to-end. The COE is one group from an organizational chart perspective. It's easy to start with this approach and then evolve to the unified or federated model over time. Cons : A centralized team might have an authoritarian tendency to favor one-size-fits-all decisions that don't always work well for all business units. There can be a tendency to prefer IT skills over business skills. Due to the centralized nature, it might be more difficult for the COE members to sufficiently understand the needs of all business units. Unified COE A unified COE is a single, centralized, shared services team that has been expanded to include embedded team members. The embedded team members are dedicated to supporting a specific functional area or business unit. Pros : There's a single point of accountability for a single team that includes cross-functional involvement from the embedded COE team members. The embedded COE team members are assigned to various areas of the business. The COE is one group from an organizational chart perspective. The COE understands the needs of business units more deeply due to dedicated members with domain expertise. Cons : The embedded COE team members, who are dedicated to a specific business unit, have a different organizational chart responsibility than the people they serve directly within the business unit. The organizational structure could potentially lead to complications, differences in priorities, or necessitate the involvement of the executive sponsor. Preferably, the executive sponsor has a scope of authority that includes the COE and all involved business units to help resolve conflicts. Federated COE A federated COE comprises a shared services team (the core COE members) plus satellite members from each functional area or major business unit. A federated team works in coordination, even though its members reside in different business units. Typically, satellite members are primarily focused on development activities to support their business unit while the shared services personnel support the entire community. Pros : There's cross-functional involvement from satellite COE members who represent their specific functional area and have domain expertise. There's a balance of centralized and decentralized representation across the core and satellite COE members. When distributed data ownership situations exist—as could be the case when business units take direct responsibility for data management activities—this model is effective. Cons : Since core and satellite members span organizational boundaries, the federated COE approach requires strong leadership, excellent communication, robust project management, and ultra-clear expectations. There's a higher risk of encountering competing priorities due to the federated structure. This approach typically involves part-time people and/or dotted line organizational chart accountability that can introduce competing time pressures. Tip Some organizations have success by using a rotational program . It involves federated members joining the core COE for a period of time, such as six months. This type of program allows federated members to learn best practices and understand more deeply how and why things are done. Although each federated member remains focused on their specific business unit, they gain a deeper understanding of the organization's challenges. This deeper understanding leads to a more productive partnership over time. Decentralized COE Decentralized COEs are independently managed by business units. Pros : A specialized data culture exists that's focused on the business unit, making it easier to learn quickly and adapt. Policies and practices are tailored to each business unit. Agility, flexibility, and priorities are focused on the individual business unit. Cons : There's a risk that decentralized COEs operate in isolation. As a result, they might not share best practices and lessons learned outside of their business unit. Collaboration with a centralized team might be informal and/or inconsistent. Inconsistent policies are created and applied across business units. It's difficult to scale a decentralized model. There's potential rework to bring one or more decentralized COEs in alignment with organizational-wide policies. Larger business units with significant funding might have more resources available to them, which might not serve cost optimization goals from an organizational-wide perspective. Important A highly centralized COE tends to be more authoritarian , while highly decentralized COEs tend to be more siloed . Each organization will need to weigh the pros and cons that apply to them to determine the best choice. For most organizations, the most effective approach tends to be the unified or federated, which bridges organizational boundaries. Funding the COE The COE might obtain its operating budget in multiple ways: Cost center. Profit center with project budget(s). A combination of cost center and profit center. When the COE operates as a cost center, it absorbs the operating costs. Generally, it involves an approved annual budget. Sometimes this is called a push engagement model. When the COE operates as a profit center (for at least part of its budget), it could accept projects throughout the year based on funding from other business units. Sometimes this is called a pull engagement model. Funding is important because it impacts the way the COE communicates and engages with the internal community. As the COE experiences more and more successes, they might receive more requests from business units for help. It's especially the case as awareness grows throughout the organization. Tip The choice of funding model can determine how the COE actively grows its influence and ability to help. The funding model can also have a big impact on where authority resides and how decision-making works. Further, it impacts the types of services a COE can offer, such as co-development projects and/or best practices reviews. For more information, see the Mentoring and user enablement article. Some organizations cover the COE operating costs with chargebacks to business units based on the usage goals of Fabric. For a shared capacity, this could be based on number of active users. For Premium capacity, chargebacks could be allocated based on which business units are using the capacity. Ideally, chargebacks are directly correlated to the business value gained. Important This article refers to Power BI Premium or its capacity subscriptions (P SKUs). Currently, Microsoft is consolidating purchase options and retiring the Power BI Premium per-capacity SKUs. New and existing customers should consider purchasing Fabric capacity subscriptions (F SKUs) instead. For more information, see Important update coming to Power BI Premium licensing and Power BI Premium FAQ . Considerations and key actions Checklist - Considerations and key actions you can take to establish or improve your COE. Define the scope of responsibilities for the COE : Ensure that you're clear on what activities the COE can support. Once the scope of responsibilities is known, identify the skills and competencies required to fulfill those responsibilities. Identify gaps in the ability to execute : Analyze whether the COE has the required systems and infrastructure in place to meet its goals and scope of responsibilities. Determine the best COE structure : Identify which COE structure is most appropriate (centralized, unified, federated, or decentralized). Verify that staffing, roles and responsibilities, and appropriate organizational chart relationships (HR reporting) are in place. Plan for future growth : If you're starting out with a centralized or decentralized COE, consider how you will scale the COE over time by using the unified or federated approach. Plan for any actions that you can take now that'll facilitate future growth. Identify customers : Identify the internal community members, and any external customers, to be served by the COE. Decide how the COE will generally engage with those customers, whether it's a push model, pull model, or both models. Verify the funding model for the COE : Decide whether the COE is purely a cost center with an operating budget, whether it will operate partially as a profit center, and/or whether chargebacks to other business units will be required. Create a communication plan : Create you communications strategy to educate the internal community of users about the services the COE offers, and how to engage with the COE. Create goals and metrics : Determine how you'll measure effectiveness for the COE. Create KPIs (key performance indicators) or OKRs (objectives and key results) to validate that the COE consistently provides value to the user community. Questions to ask Use questions like those found below to assess the effectiveness of a COE. Is there a COE? If so, who is in the COE and what's the structure? If there isn't a COE, is there a central team that performs a similar function? Do data decision makers in the organization understand what a COE does? If there isn't a COE, does the organization aspire to create one? Why or why not? Are there opportunities for federated or decentralized COE models due to a mix of enterprise and departmental solutions? Are there any missing roles and responsibilities from the COE? To what extent does the COE engage with the user community? Do they mentor users? Do they curate a centralized portal? Do they maintain centralized resources? Is the COE recognized in the organization? Does the user community consider them to be credible and helpful? Do business users see central teams as enabling or restricting their work with data? What's the COE funding model? Do COE customers financially contribute in some way to the COE? How consistent and transparent is the COE with their communication? Maturity levels The following maturity levels will help you assess the current state of your COE. Level State of the Center of Excellence 100: Initial • One or more COEs exist, or the activities are performed within the data team, BI team, or IT. There's no clarity on the specific goals nor expectations for responsibilities. • Requests for assistance from the COE are handled in an unplanned manner. 200: Repeatable • The COE is in place with a specific charter to mentor, guide, and educate self-service users. The COE seeks to maximize benefits of self-service approaches to data and BI while reducing the risks. • The goals, scope of responsibilities, staffing, structure, and funding model are established for the COE. 300: Defined • The COE operates with active involvement from all business units in a unified or federated mode. 400: Capable • The goals of the COE align with organizational goals, and they are reassessed regularly. • The COE is well-known throughout the organization, and consistently proves its value to the internal user community. 500: Efficient • Regular reviews of KPIs or OKRs evaluate COE effectiveness in a measurable way. • Agility and implementing continual improvements from lessons learned (including scaling out methods that work) are top priorities for the COE. Subscribe another address Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned. (Adobe Stock) By Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 26, 2026, 5 a.m. RELATED ARTICLE Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Andrew Deck October 17, 2026 Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry. Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday. A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” As of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences. Meta's controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 ★ Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms Legal experts and news industry leaders remain skeptical of Meta’s statements. “Publishers should always be concerned about tech companies attempting to take content for free, and should assume that Meta is taking this additional time to either find a new way to try to mislead publishers into granting Meta free access to valuable copyrighted content or finally give up in the face of pressure,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “Publishers don’t need more PR statements or explanations. They need Meta to keep its hands off their copyrighted material and respect publishers’ terms of service.” “I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.” Thomas Höppner , a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.” The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said. “My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner said. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.” News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences. On Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the company suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day. Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted. A Commission spokesperson said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Friday the the Commission has sent “its first formal requests for information under the AI Act, including to providers that have not published summaries about the data used to train their models.” “The Commission welcomes Meta’s announcement that it has postponed the entry into force of its new commercial terms,” the statement reads. “The Commission is committed to ensuring that Meta’s practices comply in full with all applicable obligations under EU law, including Article 102 TFEU and the Digital Markets Act.” In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms. “The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.” Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.” RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 “What needs to happen next is for the Competition and Markets Authority, and other regulators around the world, to secure clear, public commitments from Meta to abandon the offending elements of the new Terms before they take effect,” Bamber said. Today it's both things: The Fix Research & Advisory, working with publishers, donors and implementing organizations across Europe and beyond, and The Fix Media, a trade publication read by a community of 3,000+ senior media professionals. Our collaboration with The Fix Team has been one of the pillars in delivering on this mission, allowing us to merge academic rigour with practical, modern industry insights. Together, we have collaborated closely on our Future Media Management projects - ranging from our four-week Mini-MBA for top media executives to intensive management training for mid-level leaders. Through these programs, we have successfully trained ~ 300 media managers from 20+ countries, equipping them to navigate an increasingly complex media ecosystem. A highlight of this partnership is the delivery of the Crisis Leadership Simulation, which provides newsroom leaders with hands-on, realistic practice in managing intense operational and strategic pressure. What makes The Fix team such an exceptional partner is that they are, first and foremost, media practitioners who understand the unique constraints and challenges independent outlets face today. They bring a rare combination of Western consulting discipline and real-world experience in running newsrooms under pressure. Edgars Spuravs Director of the Anne-Marie and Gustaf Ander Centre for Media Studies at SSE Riga; Member of the Advisory Board at Journalismfund Europe; Member of Media Policy Advisory Council at Ministry of the Culture of the Republic of Latvia.

results.evidenceText: I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier said than done. | Nieman Journalism Lab Get Nieman Lab in your inbox. All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder. Subscribe another address I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier said than done. The claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right? (Adobe Stock) By Elizabeth Bromstein Oct. 26, 2026, 11:17 a.m. Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research. But I couldn’t find it. This wasn’t a totally new experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about. In this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for. I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself. Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from? Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute. Me: Great. Which study? Gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research. Me: So where did the number come from? Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense . Me: Does the book contain the original research? Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown. Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell? Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood? A breakthrough! Or so I thought Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy . Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha! I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there. Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book. I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research company Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere. Does 75% even make sense? There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job? I asked Kristen Lindquist , a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic. “I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me. There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she said. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us. So, what about that breakup? “If you get dumped and you smell some nice cookies, are you going to feel 75% better?” Lindquist said. “Probably not.” When repetition becomes evidence RELATED ARTICLE Repetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate science Yangxueqing Mary Jiang August 12, 2024 There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth. I called Jodi Schneider , an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself. “It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.” Her conclusion: “It’s hard to source.” The problem, Schneider said, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody says something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.” This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect : We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true. In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true. It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time. Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity). Meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true. Then came AI AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source. “The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.” Most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out. When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.) Nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign. That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there. I just can’t find it. Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected] . Elizabeth Bromstein is a writer, editor, and perfumer. results.evidenceText: Mozilla Foundation Fellowships 2027-2028 (up to $125,000) – Opportunity Desk Close Menu Home Conferences Training Scholarships Undergraduate Short Courses Online Courses Masters/Postgraduate PhD Postdoctoral Study Abroad Study in Africa Study in Asia Study in Australia Study in Europe Study in USA Competitions Awards Grants Fellowships Jobs Internships Volunteering Blog OD Specials OD Live Series Young Person of the Month Mentorship OD Mentors Success Stories How-To General Tips ODIC 2026 ODIC 2026 Application ODIC Judges ODIC 2025 Winners ODIC 2023 Winners ODIC 2022 Winners ODIC 2021 Winners ODIC 2019 Winners ODIC 2018 Winners ODIC 2017 Winners ODIC 2016 Winners Search Asia Africa Australia and Oceania America Europe Deadlines Approaching Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Monday, November 16 Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Instagram Telegram Mozilla Foundation Fellowships 2027-2028 (up to $125,000) Jude Ogar October 29, 2026 3 Mins Read Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Email Telegram Deadline: December 17, 2026 Applications are open for the Mozilla Foundation Fellowships 2027-2028 . Mozilla Foundation will award 10 Fellowships for the 2027–2028 period. They are looking for extraordinary individuals working at the edges of human imagination, on technology that’s too early, too unexpected, or too ambitious for anyone else to fund. Fellows are builders first, of tools and of the fields around them. But they are also defiant about who technology should serve, and rigorous about making it a reality. If that sounds like you, come build with Mozilla. Bring the wildest, most radical version of your idea: the one that questions who gets to decide and puts control back in the hands of the people who use it. Optimizing the status quo is somebody else’s job. Theirs is to build the alternatives. Fellowship Tracks The Fellowship has two tracks for builders at different stages of their careers. Both share the same commitment: developing Fellows into the kind of technology leaders a better technology future needs: Track I: Embedded Fellows – These Fellows are working on projects in collaboration with and backed by a civil society organization. Your host provides mentorship and a community to work inside. In return, you gain the experience of turning technical skill into community impact, and your host gains the expertise to advance its mission. Track II: Independent Fellows – Independent Fellows pursue their most ambitious idea in one of the areas above. You’ll turn your vision into products, working systems, and other innovations that advance better technology futures, with the freedom to choose the approach: a platform that proves an alternative model works, or tools that let other technologists build better systems. Benefits Track I: Embedded Fellows – $100,000 USD in total, as a $75,000 stipend and a $25,000 project budget. Track II: Independent Fellows – $125,000 USD in total, as a $100,000 stipend and a $25,000 project budget. Eligibility Mozilla Foundation funds projects that advance their charitable mission and create meaningful public benefit. In your application, they will ask you to describe the work you want to undertake, who stands to benefit, and what impacts you hope to see your work produce. You must be legally able to receive grant funds from Mozilla Foundation. They welcome builders from all walks and sectors to apply, and your work does not need to be focused on non-profits. They do require a charitable purpose, however. Applications must be submitted in English. Translation tools are welcome. They evaluate your ideas, not your language quality. Application Applications are reviewed through a multi-stage process. The primary review occurs at the Letter of Intent stage, with only a small number of shortlisted applicants invited to submit a full application in early 2027. Bene Fellowship 2026 (up to $30,000 CAD) Jude Ogar October 27, 2026 3 Mins Read Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Email Telegram Deadline: November 30, 2026 Applications are open for the IDRC John G. Bene Fellowship 2026 . The Bene fellowship, a bequest from the estate of John G. Bene, is offered to Canadians and permanent residents of Canada pursuing master’s or doctoral studies at a Canadian university. Candidates should have an academic background that combines an interest in forests (landscape and forest management and restoration, forestry, agroforestry), environment, ecology and food systems, with a social sciences lens (gender and inclusion, Indigenous knowledge and science, biodiversity conservation, governance of nature). This fellowship aims to facilitate practical field research on gender-responsive integrated forest, landscape and food systems restoration and management including within fire prone, degraded or disputed landscapes. Linking the broader climate-food-inclusivity nexus, it emphasizes nature-based solutions and approaches that have the potential to drive transformative change for smallholder farmers, including youth, women, and Indigenous communities in developing countries. The successful candidate will propose research that benefits less privileged people in developing countries aiming to increase the resilience of individuals and forest/agroforest communities facing difficult contexts and challenges. Note that work focused on genomics and/or genetic modification is not eligible. Grant Up to ten awards of a maximum of CA$30,000 Eligibility You must be a citizen or permanent resident of Canada; You must be enrolled at a Canadian university at the master’s or doctoral level (you must have completed several courses of the program, but not necessarily all courses, when you submit your application); You must have an academic background that combines an interest in forest, climate resilience, biodiversity or food systems. Applicants from interdisciplinary programs are eligible, provided their programs contain the specified elements; Your research proposal must be approved by your thesis supervisor and you must provide proof; Your proposed field of research must be conducted for a master’s thesis or doctoral dissertation and must take place in one or more developing countries; You must provide evidence of affiliation with an institution or organization in the developing region(s) in which the research will take place; Doctoral students must have completed coursework and passed comprehensive exams before taking up the award; and You may not be in receipt of two or more active IDRC awards at the same time, which includes the IDRC Research Awards. No time overlaps will be permitted. If you are in receipt of IDRC funds from another source (e.g. a Queen Elizabeth Advanced Scholars award or through a professor’s IDRC research grant) for activities that will still be active when and if you take up the John G. Bene Fellowship, you will be asked to demonstrate how funds from each are not being used towards the same objective. Application Click here to apply For more information, visit IDRC John G. Bene Fellowship . Share. results.pageTitle: Yale World Affairs Fellowship – Grants for Journalists
results.evidenceText: Yale World Affairs Fellowship – Grants for Journalists Skip to content View Full List Grant details View all grants Yale World Affairs Fellowship The Maurice R. Greenberg World Fellows Program is a four-month, full-time residential program based out of Yale’s International Leadership Center and housed within the Jackson School of Global Affairs . The Program runs annually from mid-August to mid-December. The Program provides World Fellows the opportunity to expand their vision, learn from each other, and grow personally and professionally. World Fellows contribute to Yale’s intellectual life, give talks and participate on panels, collaborate with peers, audit classes, and mentor students. It is NOT open to U.S. residents. Location All Locations (Open to Anyone) Funding Type Fellowship Organization Yale University School of Global Affairs Focus Area Subject Area Varies Award Size Fellows receive fully funded compensation package designed to support fellows while they are in residence at Yale Career Stage Applicants should be between five and 25 years into their professional careers, with demonstrated and significant accomplishments at a regional, national, or international level. The average age of a World Fellow is 39, though there is no minimum or maximum age limit. Editor's Note Highly competitive. They receive thousands of applications from around the globe for an extremely limited number of fellowships. Deadline 12/02/2026 Apply Here

results.title: Middle East Eye Fellowship
results.pageTitle: Middle East Eye Fellowship – Grants for Journalists
results.evidenceText: Middle East Eye Fellowship – Grants for Journalists Skip to content View Full List Grant details View all grants Middle East Eye Fellowship The Middle East Eye Fellowship is designed to support in-depth reporting by freelance journalists across the Middle East. The Fellowship program focuses each year on a theme of critical importance to the region, with applicants invited to submit detailed story pitches on the selected topic. Fellows will receive help turning their pitches into showpiece multimedia projects, while fostering broader connections within the newsroom. In 2026, Fellows explored the theme of water scarcity, with projects published from Ein al-Auja, Palestine ; Daraa, Syria, so far. The project theme for 2027 is the Rise of AI : Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used as a new tool in the machinery of oppression in the Middle East. From military targeting and securitization, to the spread of data centers, to disinformation campaigns and foreign meddling, the exploitation of AI technology is deepening inequalities and shattering lives across the region. Proof of residency will be required, with eligible countries listed on the application form; for two-person teams, at least one member must meet the residency requirements. This opportunity is reserved for freelancers and is not open to journalists in staff positions. Location Middle East Funding Type Fellowship Organization Middle East Eye Focus Area Subject Area Artificial Intelligence Award Size $1,500 Career Stage Editor's Note All freelance journalists based in the region are invited to apply. Deadline 11/01/2026 Apply Here

results.evidenceText: The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program – Grants for Journalists Skip to content View Full List Grant details View all grants The Open Notebook Early-Career Fellowship Program The Open Notebook offers a paid, part-time fellowship program for early-career science journalists. During the course of this fellowship, fellows work with a mentor to plan, report, and write articles for publication at The Open Notebook and become part of the TON editorial team. This one-year program offers fellows the opportunity to explore their career interests and passions and to sharpen their skills as part of a talented, supportive, diverse community of past and present fellows and mentors. Location Remote Funding Type Fellowship Organization The Open Notebook Focus Area Subject Area Varies Award Size $6,600 Career Stage Early career Editor's Note ideally suited for freelancers because it requires a significant weekly time commitment Deadline 10/31/2026 Apply Here
